This announcement contains a production target for the Tiris Uranium Project and forecast financial information derived from that production target. Those statements are forward-looking statements. The production target is based in part on Inferred Mineral Resources. This Cautionary Statement, the material assumptions underpinning the production target and the forecast financial information and the Competent Person statements are included in this announcement in accordance with ASX Listing Rules 5.16 and 5.17.

This announcement includes forward-looking statements. These forward-looking statements are based on the Company’s expectations and beliefs concerning future events. Forward-looking statements are necessarily subject to risks, uncertainties, and other factors, many of which are outside the control of the Company, which could cause actual results to differ materially from such statements. The Company makes no undertaking to subsequently update or revise the forward-looking statements made in this announcement, to reflect the circumstances or events after the date of this announcement.

The Company has concluded that it has a reasonable basis for providing the forward-looking statements, the production target and the forecast financial information included in this announcement, including the reasonable basis to expect that the funding required for the Project will be available when required. The reasons for that conclusion, and the material assumptions on which those statements are based, are set out in this announcement (including under “Funding”) and in Appendix 4 (Material assumptions).

The production target is based on the Mineral Resource estimate for the Tiris Uranium Project reported in accordance with the JORC Code (2012 Edition) in the ASX and AIM release dated 12 June 2024 “Aura increases Tiris’ Mineral Resources by 55% to 91.3 Mlbs U3O8”, and on the Ore Reserve estimate for the Tiris Uranium Project reported in this announcement. The Mineral Resources and Ore Reserves underpinning the production target have been prepared by a Competent Person in accordance with the requirements of the JORC Code (2012 Edition).

The material assumptions on which the production target and the forecast financial information are based, including the material assumptions about the Modifying Factors, the scheduling of development and production and the availability of project finance, are set out in Appendix 4 (Material assumptions), as required by ASX Listing Rules 5.16.1 and 5.17.1. The summary of the Ore Reserve estimate required by ASX Listing Rule 5.9.1 is set out in Appendix 2 and JORC Code Table 1 Sections 1 to 4 are set out in Appendix 3. The Competent Person statements required by ASX Listing Rules 5.16.2, 5.17.2 and 5.22 are set out under “Competent Person statement”.

The Company confirms that it is not aware of any new information or data that materially affects the information included in the ASX and AIM release dated 12 June 2024, “Aura increases Tiris’ Mineral Resources by 55% to 91.3 Mlbs U3O8”. All material assumptions and technical parameters underpinning the Mineral Resource estimates continue to apply and have not materially changed. The Company confirms that the form and context in which the Competent Person's findings are presented have not been materially modified from the original market announcement.

In accordance with ASX Listing Rule 5.16.3, the Company advises that, by ore tonnes, the production target for the Tiris Uranium Project set out in this announcement comprises 67.1% Ore Reserves (28.3% Proved Ore Reserves and 38.8% Probable Ore Reserves) and 32.9% Inferred Mineral Resources and, by contained U3O8, 67.7% Ore Reserves and 32.3% Inferred Mineral Resources. Cumulative Inferred Mineral Resources comprise less than 12% of the ore mined in the first five years of the schedule and less than 25% of the ore mined in the first ten years. Table 14 in the announcement provides details of the Ore categorisations and the periods in which they are scheduled to be mined.
No exploration target or qualifying foreign estimate is included in the production target.

The Company is also aware that ASIC has stated, in its submission to ASX and JORC dated 1 December 2011, that Inferred Mineral Resources may provide reasonable grounds in part for a statement about future matters implying economic viability where the viability of the Company's project is based on Indicated or Measured Mineral Resources (where sufficient work has been done on the Modifying Factors), Ore Reserves, or a combination of these, and where the use of Inferred Mineral Resources is not substantial. The Company understands that ASX applies this test both year by year and across the mine plan as a whole.
Consistent with that approach, the Company has scheduled the mine plan so that Inferred Mineral Resources do not form a substantial proportion of the production target in any year.

The Company is also aware that some financiers take a different approach and require Ore Reserves to be prioritised for extraction early in the mine plan. As a result, Inferred Mineral Resources could become a substantial proportion of the year-by-year production targets towards the end of the mine plan. This approach is required by some financiers to ensure that (a) Ore Reserves underpin the servicing of initial capital, which in the Company’s case would be complete by year four, (b) the present value of the project is weighted towards the material that is best understood, and (c) the Company has time to complete infill drilling to upgrade Inferred Mineral Resources to Indicated or Measured Mineral Resources ahead of their extraction.

There is a low level of geological confidence associated with Inferred Mineral Resources, and there is no certainty that further exploration work will result in the determination of Indicated Mineral Resources or that the production target itself will be realised.

The Competent Person has tested a mine plan based on Measured and Indicated Mineral Resources only (the Ore Reserve case), which produced 73.1 Mt at 226 ppm U3O8 for 36.5 Mlb over 18 years and, at a uranium price of US$90/lb U3O8, a post-tax net present value at an 8% real discount rate of about US$355.3 million and a post-tax IRR of 25%.

On that basis, the Company is satisfied that the Inferred Mineral Resources are not the determining factor in the viability of the Tiris Uranium Project. Aura intends to undertake infill drilling to convert Inferred Mineral Resources to Indicated or Measured Mineral Resources before they are scheduled to be mined, although there is no certainty that it will be able to do so.

Bankable Feasibility Study confirms Tiris as a low-cost, near-term uranium producer
Aura Energy Limited (ASX: AEE, AIM: AURA) (“Aura” or the “Company”) is pleased to announce the Bankable Feasibility Study (“BFS”) results for the Tiris Uranium Project in Mauritania (“Tiris”).

The BFS confirms Tiris as a technically simple, long-life uranium mine that requires limited capital expenditure for successful development and is expected to deliver robust returns at conservative uranium prices. The Study supports advancing the Project to a Final Investment Decision (“FID”), targeted for December 2026, with first production by the end of 2028.

Aura Energy Executive Chair, Philip Mitchell, commented:
“Tiris is a simple, robust project. It will be Mauritania’s first uranium mine and opens a new uranium province. It comes on line just as demand for uranium is accelerating.

“The BFS confirms strong returns from our first stage. Construction will cost US$350 million. Our life-of-mine cash operating cost of US$32.53 per pound U3O8 compares favourably against the global cost curve and emerging project benchmarks established in TradeTech's Independent Marketing Assessment. And we can build Tiris in two years.
“Financing arrangements are well advanced. Several strategic investors are working closely with us. We aim to select our financing partner and structure by the end of 2026.”
Aura Energy President, John Carr, commented:
“We are ready to move into execution. Engineering is complete, key permits are in place, and our owner’s team is on board. Once we make the investment decision, we can move to construction.

“A major next step will be the start-up of our continuous pilot plant at Bir Moghrein in November. The plant will process ore from each of our main ore types through the full flowsheet, validating the process under continuous operating conditions. The results will feed directly into detailed design and provide our financing partners with further confidence in the flowsheet and development plans.

“We are targeting a two-year construction period, which would put us on track to begin production by the end of 2028. We have a clear path ahead of us and are focused on executing it safely, efficiently and adopting key technologies of the digital age.”
Mauritania’s Minister of Mines and Industry, His Excellency Eddi Ould Zeine, commented:

“The Government of Mauritania strongly supports the development of Tiris, which will be our country’s first uranium mine and the foundation of a new national industry. Tiris reflects the Government’s priorities for the mining sector: a stable, predictable framework for long-term investment, and projects that create lasting value for Mauritanians.

“Through the State’s 15% interest, royalties, taxes and community contributions, the Project is expected to benefit Mauritania and its communities. Just as important are the jobs Tiris will create and Aura’s commitment to develop young Mauritanians for leadership roles in a modern, digitalised mining industry. We look forward to continuing our close cooperation with Aura as Tiris moves towards construction.”
A new uranium province: Mauritania's first uranium mine, anchoring a regional exploration position of about 13,000 km² across the Reguibat Craton.
Permitted: 30-year exploitation permits, executed Mining Conventions that stabilise fiscal terms, an approved ESIA and radiation authorisation from ARSN.

Simple to mine and process: Shallow, free-dig ore with no drilling, blasting, crushing or grinding. Over the mine’s life, scrubbing and screening recover about 91.9% of uranium, while rejecting 88% of ore mass. This reduces the leach plant's size and operating costs. The plant recovers 91.1% of uranium, giving an overall recovery of 83.7% from mined ore to final product.
Modest capital for a long life: Development capital of US$349.8 million supports a 26-year operation.
85% Renewable power: Solar and battery microgrid, externally funded via a power purchase agreement (PPA), to harness exceptional solar irradiance in region (circa. 2,200 kWh/m2 p.a.).
Autonomy and Remote Operation: Adoption of an autonomous and fully electric haulage fleet, a significant first step towards further automation to be advanced by FID.
Low development risk: Considering all these factors, TradeTech assessed Aura's Tiris as one of the lowest development-risk projects among the 'newly emerging' uranium supply.

This Announcement summarises the 2026 Bankable Feasibility Study (BFS) for the Tiris Uranium Project (Tiris or the Project) in northern Mauritania. The BFS establishes, to a bankable level of confidence, the technical viability and economic merit of developing the Eastern Tiris uranium resource. It is the basis on which Aura, its partners and prospective financiers will make a final investment decision (FID).

The BFS updates and supersedes the production targets and forecast financial information reported in the Company’s previous ASX releases. Investors should no longer rely on the production targets or forecast financial information in those earlier releases.

The Tiris ore is hosted in shallow, flat-lying calcrete. Mineralisation starts about 10 centimetres below surface. The ore zone is typically 5 to 15 metres thick. It is free-digging throughout, so no drilling or blasting is required.

The mine plan delivers 111.1 million tonnes of ore over 26 years at an average grade of 225 ppm U₃O₈. About 111.4 million tonnes of waste will also be moved, giving a strip ratio of 1.00:1. Aura will run the mine itself, using excavators and trucks across several shallow pits. Waste and tailings go back into mined-out pits, and Aura will rehabilitate the ground as mining moves on. No permanent waste dumps or tailings dams are needed.

The pits designed for the project contain 11.7 million pounds of U₃O₈ more than the mine plan extracts. All of this extra material is Inferred Mineral Resource. It sits at Marie, Hippolyte West, Hippolyte East and the southern end of Hippolyte South. Adding it would have pushed the share of Inferred material in the final years of the plan above 50%. The mine plan therefore leaves it out. Aura expects to test this material in future resource work.

Aura is also investigating methods to make the mining fleet more efficient and safer. The BFS mine plan adopts a fleet of autonomous, battery-electric haul trucks, peaking at 23 trucks, managed remotely using an autonomous haulage system (AHS). These will run around the clock and can be charged from the site’s solar power, cutting diesel use.

Future work will focus on integrating sensors into excavators, haul trucks, belts, and transfer stations, enabling ore to be scanned for geochemical and mineralogical properties prior to processing. This information would reach the plant before the ore does, allowing the Processing Plant to adjust its settings in advance to suit each load. Given the investment in the communication infrastructure with AHS, tele-remote operations for excavator, loader, and dozer will also be investigated.

First, the ore is washed and tumbled in a scrubber to break it up. It is then passed through three screens: 2 millimetres, 300 microns and, finally, 75 microns. The uranium is in the fine particles that pass through the 75-micron screen. The coarse rock left on the screen holds very little uranium, and is returned to the pit void. This step removes about 88% of ore by weight over the life-of-mine (LOM).

The beneficiation process recovers about 91.9% of the uranium and raises the grade from 225 ppm to 1,697 ppm U3O8, a seven-fold increase (life of mine average). Rejecting most of the ore mass at this stage keeps the leach plant small and operating costs low. This process occurs at one of two Beneficiation Plants, each with a design capacity of 2.5Mtpa, located near active mining sites.

The uranium-concentrated slurry is pumped to the Processing Plant as leach feed. The plant is designed to process 550,000 tonnes of leach feed per year, or about 1,500 tonnes per day, and operates at this rate in most years. Over the 26-year mine life, it averages about 520,000 tonnes per year, mainly driven by the required relocation of the beneficiation plants, which occurs seven times as mining advances into new areas. Each move, along with each shift of the mining face, briefly reduces the ore sent to the plant.

Pre-leach dewatering of the beneficiated leach feed is by two-stage centrifugation, with a wash step incorporated in the first stage. The wash rejects soluble salts and other deleterious species that would otherwise interfere with downstream processing. Centrifugation replaces the pressure filtration adopted in the previous study.
The dewatered cake then undergoes alkaline leaching, in which sodium carbonate dissolves uranium in a series of stirred tanks.

After leaching, the liquids and solids must be separated. The slurry contains dissolved uranium and very fine clay. Clay acts like a sponge, holding on to water and refusing to let go. With ordinary filters, we lose some of the uranium-bearing liquid or need huge, energy-intensive filter plants.
We now use ATA®, owned by Clean TeQ Water

, to solve this. ATA®, short for Activator-Tether-Anchor, is a complete dewatering system that conditions the clay slurry and then filters it. Its name comes from the three stages of the process (Activator-Tether-Anchor). In activation, a polymer is mixed into the leached clay slurry, where it coats and agglomerates the fine clay particles. In tethering, a second polymer is mixed into a stream of coarse desert sand, laying down a layer of binding sites across each grain. In anchoring, the two streams are combined, and the activated clay slurry bonds to the tethered sand grains, locking the fines into a granular structure. This granular structure allows the uranium-bearing liquid to drain freely rather than remain trapped within the clay particles. A horizontal vacuum belt filter is then used to separate the liquid from the solids.

This open granular structure is the key. Without ATA®, fine clay packs into a thin, tight layer that blocks the filter cloth and traps the uranium-bearing liquid. Standard chemicals (such as flocculants) can further clump clay particles together, leading to blinding of the filter cloth and entrapment of the uranium-bearing liquid. The granular structure created by ATA® further allows for efficient washing of the cake. Solution is sprayed over the cake in stages to flush out the remaining uranium-bearing liquid.

We chose ATA® for three reasons. First, it works on every type of Tiris ore. It was the only option tested that was shown to do so. Second, it does the job in one step. The previous design needed several. Third, it makes a firm, stackable cake of about 67% solids, rising to 78–79% with vibration-assisted dewatering. This means the leftover solids can go straight back into the empty mine pits.

ATA® was specifically developed to dewater fine mine tailings. Clean TeQ Water has run more than 100 bench-scale filtration tests on Tiris material. The pilot plant at Bir Moghrein, starting in November 2026, will prove ATA® on Tiris ore before the final investment decision.

Next, the uranium-bearing liquid is sent to ion exchange, where it is pumped through columns filled with resin beads. In this process, uranium is adsorbed onto resin beads. This is another key to the flowsheet. We now use Moving Bed Ion Exchange (MBIX), also from Clean TeQ Water. In MBIX, the resin beads are continuously transferred from column to column against the liquid flow, maximising resin utilisation and uranium loading. A second liquid containing sodium bicarbonate then washes the uranium off the beads in a U-shaped column, stripping out impurities and producing a concentrated uranium solution.
The uranium is then precipitated (via two stages) into a solid powder, dried, and packed into drums. This product is called yellowcake.

The final step treats the process water so that it can be reused and useful reagent chemicals can be recovered. The water is passed through nanofiltration membranes, which allow the water to pass while recovering the chemicals. One set of nanofiltration membranes recovers sodium carbonate from the waste liquid generated by ion exchange, which is then used in the leaching process, and returns it to the start of that process, reducing the amount of fresh sodium carbonate required by approximately 50%. A second set of nanofiltration membranes recovers sodium bicarbonate from the concentrated uranium stream from ion exchange, allowing it to be reused. Finally, reverse osmosis purifies the water so that the plant can reuse it.

Aura also plans to digitalise the plant and the mining operations. Enhanced instrumentation will monitor each stage of the process in real time, feeding data into a digital twin (a computer model of the plant that mirrors the behaviour of the physical operation ever more closely as the AI-driven unit process models learn from the plant’s response to changing ore characteristics and operating conditions). Operators can also use the data to test process changes before implementing them in the plant, helping to improve stability, optimise recovery and performance and identify potential issues early. The digital twin is not included in the Study's cost estimate; however, the Company aims to progress this initiative throughout the detailed design and construction phases.
The following is a summary of the key infrastructure inputs for the Project:

Renewable Power: Power and process steam will be supplied by an independent power producer (IPP) under a long-term power purchase agreement (PPA). The IPP will fund, build, own and operate the generation facility, so power generation carries no development capital for Aura and is included in operating costs. Based on a request-for-proposal process with several large power providers, a power price of US$0.15/kWh and $92/t steam (via diesel boilers) has been used in the study. Prior to execution of a PPA, Aura will work with potential IPPs to produce steam by renewables.

Water: The Taoudeni bore field can sustainably supply up to 74 litres per second, with C22 available as a supplementary supply, against a site requirement of 56 litres per second. A bore field and water pipeline from the Taoudeni basin (120km south of the Project) has been included in the BFS capital and operating estimate.
Access: Product is trucked about 1,447 km to the Port of Nouakchott, of which 782 km is sealed highway. Rail via the SNIM line has been assessed and remains open for further optimisation.

Every decision we make about the physical assets (mining, processing, infrastructure) takes the nature of human work into consideration. Our objective is to provide Mauritania with the first mining and processing operation of a new age where the jobs on offer provide staff with excellent career development opportunities, intellectual stimulation and quality of life.

Safer work: Autonomous mining and plant digitalisation allow the handover of relentlessly repetitive tasks from humans to machines. Exposure to physically and mentally harmful working conditions can be sharply reduced. And because a lean site crew can be supervised from an operations centre in Nouakchott, fewer people need to live away from their families in a remote and often harsh environment.

Better careers: Roles can be refocused on problem-solving and decision-making, becoming higher-value-adding, better-paid, and forming the foundation of attractive careers. Over time, such skills improve the quality of individual lives. They will also help strengthen Mauritania's broader economy.

Higher productivity: There is no trade-off between the human benefits and business performance. Machines don't get bored, so they perform repetitive tasks with greater predictability. Better jobs attract, motivate and retain better people. And the gains compound: the plant's models learn and never forget with every tonne processed, and one operations centre can oversee several plants at once.

Mauritania shares in the value of Tiris at every level of the Project: through royalties on revenue, wages paid to the workforce, community contributions, tax on profits and the State’s dividends from its 15% interest. Over the 26-year mine life, the Project is expected to generate about US$4,115 million of revenue. Of the US$2,042 million of surplus cash flow (revenue less operating costs, capital and closure costs), about US$903 million, or 44%, is expected to flow to the Government of Mauritania and local communities.
Royalties: 3.5% of the FOB value of product sold, payable from first production regardless of profitability. About US$143 million over the mine life, or US$5.5 million a year.

Jobs: A peak construction workforce of about 600 people on site (including Aura’s owner’s team) and about 438 operating roles (381 at commencement of operations) across site, Nouakchott and Zouérat. Wages of about US$191 million over the mine life are included in operating costs.
Communities: Community contributions of about US$35.6 million over the mine life, included in all-in sustaining cost.

Tax: Corporate tax of 25% after a 36-month tax holiday. Tax is first paid in 2036, once construction-related tax losses are used, and totals about US$377 million, or about US$18.9 million a year over the 20 years in which it is paid. Withholding tax of 10% on dividends paid to Aura adds about US$126 million.
State dividends: ANARPAM’s 15% free-carried interest is expected to receive about US$222 million in dividends from surplus cash flow.

Development capital has risen from US$230 million to US$349.8 million, mainly because the process plant has been re-estimated based on more advanced engineering in the 2025 Basic Engineering and this Study; mining equipment is now purchased rather than leased and includes the provision for autonomy and remote operation; escalation on purchased items; and contingency is higher on an absolute basis. Sustaining capital is now fully costed over the life of mine. Operating costs are higher, primarily due to increased reagent consumption and rising reagent unit costs, as well as an increased allowance for site G&A.
These increases reflect a higher level of engineering definition, not a change in the underlying Project, which the pilot plant is intended to confirm before FID.

The Study assumes US$400 million of funding (Table 5) comprising US$220 million (55%) of debt, being US$170 million of senior project debt and US$50 million of subordinated debt, and US$180 million (45%) of equity, royalties or other quasi-equity instruments. This covers the peak funding requirement of US$379.6 million, including US$38.6 million of contingency, and leaves US$20.4 million of debt undrawn at first production.

The Study’s debt assumptions are conservative. All debt is assumed to bear an interest rate of 9%, with all the necessary finance arrangement fees and transaction costs included in the financial analysis. Cash margins are robust, underpinned by a C1 Cash Cost of US$32.53/lb against a realised price of US$89.3/lb. Under this base case scenario, the minimum annual debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) is 2.23x, loan life coverage ratio of 2.56x, and peak debt at 1.6x EBITDA, thus signalling significant headroom.

Aura is in advanced discussions with the US International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) on approximately US$150–170 million of senior debt and has received a non-binding, fully funded proposal from a major US investment fund. Separately, on 2 June 2026, Aura signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding (MOU) with a major international nuclear utility covering a potential strategic equity investment and related funding support, a framework for offtake discussions, and technical collaboration including a confirmatory due diligence pilot plant. Aura retains full ownership and operational control of the Project, with any participation rights linked to a defined funding contribution. The parties’ indicative timetable targets a commercial agreement by 31 December 2026 and any required approvals by 30 June 2027. The MOU is non-binding and thus subject to due diligence, credit and investment committee approvals, and definitive documentation.

With respect to these funding discussions, Aura is not yet locked into any lender, investor, or funding strategy, as the optimal strategy is conditional upon the completion of this Study. To this end, future funding plans are indicative only. The Company has a reasonable basis to believe the required funding will be available when needed, based on the Project economics, payback and credit metrics detailed within this report.

Tiris has not yet contracted most of its production. About 83% of the expected yearly output remains available. This leaves Aura free to offer it as part of a transaction with a strategic offtaker. The only currently effective long-term contract is a small offtake with Curzon Uranium (Curzon), which covers 300,000lb a year. Aura will sell half of this at fixed prices that rise from US$60.3 to US$67.8 per lb if FID occurs before the end of 2026, or US$59.0 to US$66.5 per lb if FID occurs before the end of 2027. Aura will sell the other half at the spot price minus a 5% discount. The study assumes that all uncontracted production sells at the spot price. On this basis, assuming a flat US$90/lb price, Aura expects to receive an average of US$89 a pound over the mine life.

The principal approvals required to develop the Project have been granted, with a number of routine construction and operating permits expected to be granted in a timely manner. The BFS keeps the production base broadly unchanged but re-bases costs on the current engineering. It also reflects three technical changes that materially reshape the Project:

Dewatering: The fine fraction of Tiris ore is dominated by active clays. The finer 75 μm screen cut adopted for the BFS, in place of 150 μm, concentrates these clays in the leach feed. The Project lies in the north-eastern, Palaeoproterozoic part of the Reguibat Shield, within the West African Craton. The shield is made up mainly of granites, metasediments and metavolcanics. It is bounded by the Taoudeni Basin to the south, the Tindouf Basin to the north and the Mauritanide fold belt to the west.

Two main granite types occur in the resource areas. A grey granite carries about 1–2 ppm uranium. A finer-grained, foliated red granite carries 5–20 ppm uranium and is thought to be the source of the uranium in the deposits.

The resource areas lie under very flat ground, covered by desert pavement and thin wind-blown sand. The uranium occurs in weathered red granite and in gravels laid down on or near it. The mineralised gravels and weathered granite sit at the surface or under less than 30 cm of sand. They form thin, flat, continuous sheets 1 to 12 m thick over fresh granite.

The uranium occurs as carnotite, a potassium uranium vanadate, possibly with some of the related calcium mineral tyuyamunite. The carnotite is mostly micron-scale. It forms fine dustings and coatings on granite fragments and in patches of calcium carbonate (calcrete).
Figure 7: Typical trench showing soft sandy overburden over gravelly, free-digging calcrete ore

The deposits formed as saline groundwater leached uranium from the red granites during wetter periods over the past 2.5 million years. The most recent wet period ended about 5,900 years ago. Evaporation in the following dry periods precipitated the uranium vanadates together with carbonates, sulphates and chlorides.

Tiris differs from better-known calcrete uranium deposits such as Langer Heinrich in Namibia and Yeelirrie in Western Australia. Those are river valley-fill deposits in clays or hard calcrete below the water table. Tiris formed in shallow depressions in loose gravels and weathered granite, above the water table.

This is why the ore is loose and lies at or near the surface, so it can be dug without blasting and needs no crushing. The carnotite forms fine coatings on the gravel and granite fragments, so it separates readily from the host rock.

The main economic drivers of the Tiris flowsheet are the extent of ore upgrading during screening and the management of sulphate that reaches the leach. Geometallurgical domaining predicts how these drivers vary across the resource. The domains are carried into the Mineral Resource block models, the recovery estimates and the mine plan.

The 2019 DFS test work used three process-behaviour composites built from a 2018 trench programme at Lazare North and Lazare South. For the BFS, AMC Consultants rebuilt the domaining across the whole resource using the larger assay, mineralogy and screening dataset. The new domaining is now the primary framework for the Project.

AMC applied a multivariate statistical method (UMAP) to calcium, aluminium and sulphur assays, which separate material mainly by its calcite, silicate and gypsum (sulphate) content. Combined with mineralogy and screening results, Aura has defined three domains:
Domain 1 – calcium-rich. Low aluminium and sulphur; quartz, feldspar, and calcite; represents 16.1% of the mine plan. Forms the surface layer.
Domain 2 – sulphur-rich. High sulphur, calcium and strontium from gypsum; represents 23.2% of the mine plan. Sits beneath Domain 1 where present and varies in thickness.

Domain 3 – aluminium-rich. High aluminium, phosphorus and potassium, low sulphur and calcium; mainly quartz and feldspar; represents 60.7% of the mine plan. Forms the base of the sequence and the majority of material mined in the first years of operation.
Uranium grade shows no correlation with the domains, indicating that all three are similarly mineralised.

Tiris will be mined by conventional, owner-operated open-cut methods. The ore is shallow, flat-lying and free-digging, so no drilling or blasting is needed. Most mineralisation lies within 6 to 8 m of surface. Excavators and wheel loaders will load road-style tipper trucks, which haul ore a short distance to the nearest beneficiation plant.

No permanent waste dumps or tailings dams are needed. Waste, coarse beneficiation rejects, and dry-filtered tailings are all returned to mined-out pits. Tailings are placed at the base of the pits and covered with rejects and waste. Clean sand is also mined to support post-leach dewatering (see “Processing”).
The mine plan uses two relocatable beneficiation plants, moved seven times over the mine life as mining moves between deposits. Hippolyte East and West ore is hauled to the Hippolyte North plant.

Metallurgical test work on Tiris ore has run continuously since 2011, across 27 test programmes. Laboratories and vendors include ANSTO Minerals, RCS/Acclarium, Clean TeQ Water, Vietti Slurrytec, ENPROTEC and Jord International. The BFS adopts an overall recovery from ore mined to final product of 83.7% as an average over the life of mine. Beneficiation recovers 91.9% of the uranium, and the hydrometallurgical plant recovers 91.1% of the uranium in the leach feed average of the LOM, or 91.5% at steady state.

Uranium is hosted solely in carnotite, with grains finer than 5 μm that are well liberated by scrubbing. The gangue is dominated by carbonate minerals (calcite and strontianite), with sulphate minerals (gypsum and celestine) and clays. Because carbonate minerals dominate, alkaline leaching is preferred to acid leaching, which would consume large amounts of acid.

The breakthrough for Tiris was finding that screening concentrates most of the carnotite into a small fine fraction. Screening the washed ore recovers more than 91% of the uranium into 12% of the ore mass (life of mine average) at a cut size of 75 µm. Sulphate minerals, which consume leach reagent, tend to report to the coarse fraction and are rejected. In the plant, trucks tip ore over a 200 mm grizzly into a feed hopper. No feeder-breaker is needed because the ore is loose. A rotating drum scrubber washes the carnotite off the coarser particles in about one minute. A hydrocyclone recovers water from the fine-screen oversize. A thickener at each beneficiation plant recovers more water before the slurry is pumped to the Processing Plant. Each beneficiation plant (2.5Mtpa design capacity) is built as modules on skids or trailers, so it can be moved. The mine schedule allows 30 days of downtime for each move.

Alkaline leaching with sodium carbonate and bicarbonate at 80°C extracted 96% of the uranium from the Lazare composites. Most extraction occurred within four hours, and the design residence time is 12 hours. Sodium carbonate consumption rises in line with the sulphate content of the leach feed. The plant leaches in six stirred tanks in series. Hot slurry leaving the leach heats the incoming feed by direct contact. This avoids heat exchangers, which would scale up. The same method is used at Langer Heinrich. Steam injection supplies the rest of the heat.

The combination of a finer screen cut and the mix of geometallurgical domain ore in feed can send more clay to the leach. The clays in the fine fraction are about 90% illite and mica, which consolidate poorly and break down further during leaching. Test work found that clay stability, and with it dewatering performance, is impacted by the salinity (total dissolved solids) of the process solution.

Pressure filters could form competent cakes only with a silica additive at up to half the solids mass. At the finer cut, the Project would have needed six very large filter presses ahead of the leach and thirteen after it, adding significant cost to the process. Pressure filtration was therefore replaced:

Before the leach – two-stage decanter centrifuges. Bench spin tests produced clear water and cakes of 47–52% solids. Two stages reduce chloride below the 2 g/L limit needed for ion exchange. Each stage has three units. Recycled sodium carbonate is added between the stages. It turns gypsum into sodium sulphate, which dissolves and is washed out before the leach. This reduces the amount of fresh sodium carbonate needed.

After the leach – ATA conditioning and three horizontal vacuum belt filtration (HVBF) units, operating in parallel. Clean TeQ Water's Activator-Tether-Anchor (ATA®) chemistry binds the fine clays to added coarse sand, forming a free-draining structure that washes and filters well. It produces a stackable cake of about 67% solids in one step, rising to 78–79% with Jord International's Viper vibration technology. Counter-current wash tests recovered 97.6–97.8% of the soluble uranium.

ATA+HVBF was the only option shown to be robust across the full range of ore variability. While ATA has not yet been used at a commercial uranium operation, the use of HVBF is common in the mining industry. Clean TeQ Water has run more than 100 bench filtration tests on Tiris material and is delivering a 750,000 t/y ATA+HVBF plant at the Rasp mine at Broken Hill.
The pilot plant operation, to commence in November, also includes two-stage centrifugation for pre-leach and HVBF and ATA on post-leach to confirm the assumptions on Tiris ore.

Uranium is recovered from the leach solution by moving-bed ion exchange (MBIX), using Clean TeQ Water's continuous system. It replaces the fixed-bed ion exchange assumed in earlier studies.  MBIX improves solids tolerance, resin use and reagent and water consumption.

The MBIX circuit has four columns. Resin moves between them by airlift about once an hour. The uranium is eluted with sodium bicarbonate and precipitated with sodium hydroxide as sodium diuranate. It is then purified and precipitated again as uranium peroxide. The product is dried in a fluid-bed dryer and packed into drums in a secure building. Test work product met ASTM specifications.

The Tiris Optimised Pilot Plant (TOPP) is a purpose-built, modular demonstration plant at Bir Moghrein that replicates the full commercial Tiris flowsheet at pilot scale, at about 1/470th of the commercial plant’s mass throughput. The flowsheet employs proven and widely used mineral processing and uranium recovery technologies, making TOPP a confirmation programme instead of a technology development project.

The pilot plant is a small copy of the full plant. It runs the principal processing steps in series. First, the ore is washed and screened. Then the uranium is dissolved out. Then the solids are filtered off. Finally, the uranium is collected from the liquid. Water and reagents are cleaned and reused, just as they will be in the full plant. Product purification of the eluate into uranium oxide concentrate will be undertaken at a licensed laboratory outside Mauritania to demonstrate product quality to prospective offtake partners.
More than 80 tonnes of Tiris ore will be tested. Some comes from each main ore type. The rest is a mix that matches the ore planned for the first five years. The pilot is built in two parts:

Module A – beneficiation and pre-leach dewatering: scrubbing, screening and centrifuge dewatering at up to 1 t/h upgrade the ore, rejecting about 90% of the mass as barren residue and concentrating the uranium into a small, high-grade leach feed; and

Module B – hydrometallurgy: carbonate leach, ATA and horizontal vacuum belt filtration, MBIX recovery and nanofiltration reagent recycle, operated at about 150 kg/h to prove out the recycle and impurity build-up behaviour that carries most of the process risk;

Earth Systems prepared the original Environmental and Social Impact Assessment (ESIA), which was lodged in May 2017 and approved in October 2017. In accordance with good practice, and due to the growth of the project’s scale, Aura worked with the Ministry of Environment to submit a revised ESIA in 2025. The Project is in a hyper-arid, uninhabited part of the Sahara, historically a military zone. There are no permanent settlements, protected areas or critical habitat nearby, no surface water use and no need for resettlement. The nearest Important Bird Area, at Chegga, is about 130–159 km away and is not affected by water abstraction. A 2026 archaeological survey of the plant, camp, airstrip and water pipeline corridor, and selected areas at Sadi and Hippolyte, found no archaeological remains within any planned infrastructure footprint; ten sites (nine protohistoric tumuli and one Muslim grave) lie alongside the footprints and are to be preserved. A heritage monitoring MOU was signed with IMRFPC in February 2026.

The ESIA concludes that residual impacts after mitigation are mostly low or lower, and none are rated high. A small number are rated moderate: dust during operations, road transport of product, occupational health and safety, and groundwater demand. Economic development is rated moderate positive.

Uranium ore is naturally occurring radioactive material. The Project creates no new radiation sources. The ore is low in thorium, and the product is a stable oxide transported as Class 7 material. Radiation protection follows the ICRP principles through a Radiation Management Plan approved under Mauritania's Nuclear Energy Law.

Knight Piésold found no groundwater-dependent ecosystems or existing users in the borefield areas. Community water points within about 40 km down-gradient could see minor drawdown. All final pit floors sit above the water table, and dry tailings placed in the pits are predicted to have negligible impact on groundwater. A groundwater radiological baseline is underway, and potable water will be monitored for uranium and radioactivity.

Closure is primarily achieved through progressive backfilling. Fine tailings are buried at the base of mined-out pits and covered with coarse rejects and waste, returning surface radiation to below pre-mining levels. Landforms are then graded and revegetated with local species chosen with nomadic groups. Modular plant and camp buildings are removed at closure. The design goal is no permanent change to the natural landform. Closure and rehabilitation costs of US$20 million are included in the Financial Model.

The Environmental and Social Management and Monitoring Plan sits over a suite of management plans covering radiation, closure, stakeholder engagement, transport, occupational health and safety, emergency response and security. Plans for water, waste, greenhouse gas, tailings, air quality, chemicals and biodiversity are being prepared.

Stakeholders include national and regional government, ANARPAM, the military, nomadic herders, artisanal miners at Gleib Ndour and the Zouérat community. A grievance mechanism aligned with IFC standards is in place.

Our ambition for Tiris is bigger than a single well-run mine. We aim to build a first predictable business, with a plant that reconciles itself to the ore it receives and learns from every tonne it processes. Beyond that, we aim to build a repeatable system for developing a new uranium province, anchored by Aura's exploration position across northern Mauritania. The system has three parts. Each is built once at Tiris and carried to every deposit that follows.

The method: Tiris is already designed to repeat itself. Its beneficiation plants relocate seven times over the mine life as mining advances. Aura intends the process models, data architecture and digital twin to move with them. A new deposit would then start from models already trained on the province's ore, not from a blank page. Each move should make the next one faster, cheaper and less risky.

The people: Mauritanians who learn their trade at Tiris become the leaders and specialists of the operations that follow. Each new deposit draws on a larger and more experienced national workforce than the last. The skills largely stay in Mauritania.

The place: The remote operations centre, likely in Nouakchott, and the Technology Centre we are also considering are designed to serve more than one plant. One centre can, in time, supervise several operations at once, so new deposits increase output without adding a new layer of overhead.

For Mauritania, the value of Tiris therefore lies beyond the royalties, taxes and dividends set out above. It lies in a national capability to develop the country's uranium endowment, increasingly led by Mauritanians. Future deposits do not form part of this Study, and there is no certainty that further exploration will result in additional Mineral Resources or operations.

Nuclear power is entering a period of sustained growth. At COP28 in 2023, more than 20 countries pledged to triple nuclear capacity by 2050, and the International Energy Agency counts more than 70 GW of reactors under construction. Electrification and data-centre demand add to this. The World Nuclear Association expects reactor requirements to rise from about 69,000 t U (179 Mlb U3O8) in 2025 to more than 150,000 t U (390 Mlb U3O8) by 2040.

Supply is not keeping pace. Primary production of about 157 Mlb U3O8 in 2024 was highly concentrated, with the top five countries supplying about 85%. Many of the largest mines deplete during the 2030s, and new mines now take 8 to 15 years to develop. The World Nuclear Association estimates that 49–60% of 2040 demand will need to come from mines not yet built. TradeTech estimates that the share of Western supply producible below US$25/lb falls from 69% in 2028 to 38% in 2030.

Security of supply is also driving demand for new production from stable jurisdictions. Uranium is on the United States critical minerals list, and restrictions on Russian-origin enriched uranium are in place.

Proved Ore Reserves are derived from Measured Mineral Resources and Probable Ore Reserves from Indicated Mineral Resources. No Inferred material is included in the Ore Reserve. Of the Ore Reserve, 31.5 Mt at 237 ppm for 16.4 Mlb is Proved and 43.1 Mt at 219 ppm for 20.8 Mlb is Probable.

Conventional, owner-operated open-cut mining with excavators, wheel loaders and off-road trucks. The ore is free-digging, so no drilling or blasting is required. Pits are shallow and progressively backfilled with waste, beneficiation rejects, and filtered tailings, so no pit-slope geotechnical work was required. Mining panels of at least 100 m × 100 m were defined from Whittle optimisation shells. Dilution and ore loss are applied by excluding resource blocks with less than 4% mineralisation, reflecting a smallest mining unit of about 200 t.

Ore is scrubbed and wet screened at 75 μm in relocatable beneficiation plants. The fine fraction is pumped to a central plant, dewatered by two-stage centrifuges and leached in sodium carbonate and bicarbonate at about 80°C. Leached solids are separated by ATA-conditioned belt filtration, and uranium is recovered by moving-bed ion exchange, precipitated and packaged. Recoveries are applied by geometallurgical group: beneficiation metal loss of 11% (Group 1), 15.0% (Group 2) and 4.1% (Group 3), and processing recovery of 91.5% for all groups. Beneficiation mass yield to leach feed is 21.4% (Group 1), 11.7% (Group 2) and 9.9% (Group 3).
A cut-off grade of 100 ppm U3O8 is applied to Groups 2 and 3, and 150 ppm to Group 1, based on calculated break-even cut-offs of 100, 80, and 151 ppm, respectively.

The Ore Reserve is based on the June 2024 MIK recoverable resource models prepared by H&S Consultants, coded with defined geometallurgical groups. Whittle optimisations were run on Measured and Indicated material only. Revenue factor 0.9 shells returned 69.1 Mt at 236 ppm for 35.9 Mlb, within 7% of the December 2024 Ore Reserve.

The uranium mineralisation generally forms thin shallow horizontal tabular bodies ranging in thickness from 1 to 12m hosted in weathered granite and granitic sediments. Differentiation of the weathered granite from granitic sediments is unreliable from air-core sample returns.

HSC generated surfaces representing the base of the mineralisation at each deposit in order to limit the extrapolation of grades into volumes that have no data. This is important at Tiris as there is a general decrease in uranium grades with depth.

These basal surfaces generally represent the top of fresh granite, where air-core drilling could penetrate no further. The basal surfaces were produced using the locations of the end of the deepest assay from each drill hole.

The exceptions are the 2022 air-core drilling, when a hydraulic hammer was used instead of a conventional blade bit, and all diamond core holes. Therefore, these holes could penetrate fresh rock, while the blade bit used in other years could not. This difference is important to the Tiris project because the DFS assumes that mining will be free-digging. Consequently, fresh rock intersected in the 2022 air-core holes and all diamond core drilling will not be mineable under current assumptions and needs to be excluded from the MRE. Therefore, in deposits with 2022 air-core holes and diamond core drilling (Sadi, Lazare South and Hippolyte North), an additional surface was created to represent the top of fresh rock, which may be shallower than the base of mineralisation in places.
Areas of obvious outcrop were excised from the MRE assuming a dip of 45 degrees between weathered granite/granitic sediments and the fresh granite.

HSC used the locations of all drill hole collars that had been located with the DGPS to create a wireframe representing the topographic surface. The elevations of all drill holes that had been located using a handheld GPS were then derived from this topographic surface.

Uranium concentration was estimated by recoverable Multiple Indicator Kriging (MIK) using GS3 geostatistical software. The uranium grades at the Tiris deposits exhibit a positively skewed distributions and therefore show reasonable sensitivity to a small number of high grades. MIK is considered an appropriate estimation method for the uranium grade distribution at the Tiris deposits because it specifically accounts for the changing spatial continuity at different grades through a set of indicators variograms at a range of grade thresholds. It also reduces the need to use the practice of top cutting.

The resource area composite samples on which these metallurgical results is based is from Aura’s trench sampling program completed in 2018 across the Lazare North and Lazare South Resources. (ASX release: Quarterly report June 2018 and Appendix 5B, 31st July 2018). Trench locations were selected to correspond to diamond drill (DD) locations from 2017 drilling program (ASX Release: Tiris Resource upgrade success, 30 April 2018) as reported in ASX release: Quarterly report June 2018 and Appendix 5B, 31st July 2018. A total of 11 trenches were excavated (8 Lazare South and 3 Lazare North) to a depth of 4m. Trenches were oriented west to east and sampling was undertaken by channel sampling of north and south walls at 0.5m depth intervals. Interval samples were not split on site. Trench interval samples were split at Aura Energy’s Nouakchott laboratory by rotary splitter divider (RSD). A minimum 2kg sub sample was collected for assay, a 1kg sub sample was collected for geometallurgical test work, a 2kg sample was collected for reference and the remainder was stored as inputs for bulk metallurgical composite preparation. Given the fine grained nature of the uranium minerals these sample sizes are appropriate. Subsamples for assay were sent to ALS Minerals, Nouakchott, where they were crushed by a jaw crusher to -12mm and 1kg was riffle split for pulverising to +85% passing 75 microns. An c. 100g split was bagged and sent for analysis by pressed pellet XRF. Previous analysis comparing different analytical methods (XRF, ICP, DNC) had indicated that XRF is an accurate method on this material, if an x-ray band is selected for measurement that is not affected by the presence of strontium, and this was done. This method will measure total uranium. A sub-split of assay samples was prepared by ALS Laboratories Nouakchott by Method Prep 22 (Crush to 70% less than 6mm, pulverize entire sample to better than 85% passing 75 microns). An c. 100g sample of pulp was split off using mini-riffle splitter, placed in sample envelope and forwarded by air to ALS in Ireland for uranium analysis by ALS Method U-MS62 (U by ICP-MS after 4 acid digestion). 4 acid digestion provides near total extraction. Geometallurgical samples for each interval were screened at 1mm, 300µm, 150µm and 75µm and fractions weighed and assayed by portable XRF. A split of the -75µm fraction for each interval was collected by RSD and sent to ALS Minerals for uranium analysis by ALS Method U-MS62 (U by ICP-MS after 4 acid digestion). 4 acid digestion provides near total extraction. The results of assay and geometallurgical analysis were analysed to define process behaviour based geometallurgical domains. Three domains were identified (2 x Lazare South and 1 x Lazare North). These formed the basis for generation of bulk composite samples for metallurgical test work. Interval samples were sent to Australian MinMet Metallurgical Laboratories (AMML), Gosford, Australia where they were combined based on composite definitions and mixed by rolling barrel. The uranium market is currently in a structural supply deficit. Following the post-Fukushima period of oversupply, sustained low prices disincentivised resource development while climate and energy security policy returned reactor requirements to pre-Fukushima levels by around 2019, moving the market into deficit. The deficit is not confined to uranium: conversion and enrichment are also in deficit, a rare simultaneous condition across all three front-end fuel cycle components. Restrictions on the delivery of Russian enriched uranium product to the USA and Europe, with Russian nuclear fuel prohibited from entry into the USA from January 2028, have segmented the market and widened the deficit facing Western utilities.

A significant future increase in nuclear generation capacity is expected. Nuclear power currently accounts for approximately 10% of global electricity and around 30% of low-carbon generation. China is expected to nearly double its nuclear generation capacity by 2040 according to the China Nuclear Energy Association, and in March 2026 Belgium, Brazil, China and Italy endorsed the Declaration to Triple Global Nuclear Capacity by 2050, bringing the number of supporting nations to 38. Policy support has strengthened materially, including US Department of Energy financing of US$17.5 billion to accelerate ten new large reactors, Canadian plans for ten new reactors by 2040, inclusion of nuclear power in the European Union green taxonomy, and reversal of planned early reactor retirements in the USA. Demand from high-intensity electricity users, including data centre operators pursuing small modular reactors, represents a new category of consumer.

The increase in nuclear generation capacity will require a significant increase in uranium mine production. Successive supply-side delays, curtailments to planned production and diminished exploration activity stand at odds with steadily increasing requirements and reduced available supply.  Long-term price forecasts have the weighted average term price exceeding US$90/lb U3O8 in 2026 and remaining between the mid-US$90s and US$105/lb U3O8 in real terms through to 2035. Sufficient new projects are assessed to become competitive as the weighted average term price approaches the US$55 to US$60/lb U3O8 level, and utilities have shown a greater willingness to commit to long-term contracts at prices that capture future production costs.
